PARIS — Top European defense ministers and EU representatives said Ukraine faces challenging months ahead, insisting they must keep supporting Kyiv despite the U.S. bid for talks with Russia.
"The new diplomatic push is there, but it's also clear that Putin's actions tell a different story," the EU's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said at a press conference in Paris on Monday. Kallas said she was expecting a "brutal winter" for Kyiv and that there was "no hope for imminent peace," reiterating the need to help Ukraine "withstand the attacks and increase the cost for Russia."
Kallas, along with European Commissioner for Defence and Space Andrius Kubilius, joined a meeting with defense ministers from the E5 group made up of France, the U.K., Germany, Poland and Italy, hosted at the French armed forces ministry.

articles.title: West warns of famine risk in Sudan as civil war grinds on - BBC
articles.summary: West warns of famine risk in Sudan as civil war grinds on  BBCUS, European powers warn of worsening hunger crisis in Sudan as over 5 million face food insecurity  Business Insider AfricaUS, dozens of countries warn of Sudan famine risk, urge aid  ReutersA War-Torn Nation Is on the Brink of Famine  NewserFood and Hope in Sudan  Send Relief
articles.full_text:
The US and 30 other Western states have warned of an "alarming deterioration" in food security in Sudan, urging the warring sides in the civil war to remove obstacles to humanitarian aid to prevent famine.
In a joint statement, the signatories said conflict was the main driver of Sudan's hunger crisis, damaging critical infrastructure and disrupting food production.
"There is very little to survive on," Yusuf Roble, regional director for Islamic Relief East Africa, told BBC Newsday, describing how people returning to Omdurman were finding their homes destroyed or looted.
The war, which began in April 2023, has displaced 14 million people.
The statement was signed by EU states, the UK, Canada, Switzerland and Norway, as well as the US, where it was published by the state department on Monday after first appearing on the European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations website.
It estimates that 19.5 million people or 41% of Sudan's population are experiencing high levels of acute food insecurity, including five million facing emergency levels of hunger.
"I met a mother of seven children who doesn't really know the whereabouts of her husband for the last three and a half years and he was the breadwinner, the sole breadwinner for the family," Roble said.
While the war in Sudan has led to what the World Health Organization has described as the world's worst humanitarian crisis, Roble said only 40% of Sudan's 2026 humanitarian needs plan had been funded as of September.
"Their meals come from the community kitchen, which doesn't really even have very long-term support because of funding cuts," Roble added.
The joint statement warns that "the number of children suffering from severe acute malnutrition could exceed the projected 825,000" without immediate action.
The crisis is being exacerbated by what the signatories describe as systematic obstruction of aid and the effects of El Niño, which has reduced rainfall and increased drought across more than half of Sudan.
"The parties to the conflict bear primary responsibility for alleviating the suffering of the Sudanese people," the statement says, urging them to lift all impediments to humanitarian assistance and allow full, safe, rapid and unimpeded access.
In June, the UN-backed Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, a measure of the severity and magnitude of food crises, estimated that 5.1 million people in Sudan faced severe hunger.
The civil war in Sudan began in April 2023 following a power struggle between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.

U.K. Chancellor John Healey is set to announce an unexpected increase in defense spending in his first budget on Wednesday. The move aims to bring Britain closer to NATO's defense targets amid public concerns over military readiness and marks an early policy push for Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government.
The budget is expected to address a £4.7 billion deficit in military funding as part of the Defence Investment Plan to modernize the armed forces. Officials view the funding boost as a down payment toward Britain's goal of spending 3 percent of gross domestic product on defense by 2030, ahead of NATO's broader 3.5 percent target by 2035.
Healey faces narrow financial margins due to government spending rules and debt limits. The full path toward meeting the 3.5 percent NATO target is expected to be outlined in next year's spending review.
The financial constraints have drawn criticism from Parliament. Member of Parliament Mike Martin argued that fiscal limits restrict the administration's options: "They have got themselves into a straitjacket over defense spending and none of this will be resolved before the next election. This is why I think an early general election is inevitable."
Alongside direct state funding, the government is seeking to unlock private capital for the domestic defense sector. Plans include allocating £15.4 billion to the National Wealth Fund and £5 billion to the British Business Bank, with portions potentially supporting defense firms. A formal Defence Finance and Investment Strategy is scheduled for December following an investment summit on Dec. 1.
Britain has also opted against joining the Canadian-led Defence, Security and Resilience Bank, focusing instead on its own Multilateral Defence Mechanism with £400 million allocated for joint procurement and stockpiling. In technology, the Treasury announced £165 million for artificial intelligence-driven detection of biological threats and £60 million for the Sovereign AI fund to invest in British tech firms.

articles.title: India opposes ‘Second-Class’ status for new UN security council members - Daijiworld
articles.summary: India opposes ‘Second-Class’ status for new UN security council members  Daijiworld
articles.full_text:
Daijiworld Media Network - New Delhi
New Delhi, Oct 27: India has asserted that any reform of the United Nations Security Council that creates a new category of permanent members without veto powers would relegate them to “second-class” status, leaving the existing five permanent members in control of decision-making.
Addressing the Inter-Governmental Negotiations (IGN) plenary on the question of the veto at the UN General Assembly on Monday, India's Permanent Representative to the UN, Ambassador Harish Parvathaneni, said all permanent members of a reformed Security Council must have veto powers as long as the provision continues to exist.
China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States are the five permanent members of the 15-member Security Council and enjoy veto powers. The remaining 10 members are elected for two-year terms.
Parvathaneni said creating another category of long-term members without veto powers would not alter the decision-making dynamics of the existing five permanent members, commonly known as the P5. He added that creating a new category of permanent members, with or without veto powers, would complicate negotiations and deepen the inequalities that reform efforts seek to address.
“Periodic elections and the concept of permanency are fundamentally contradictory,” the diplomat said.
Recalling the only expansion of the Security Council in 1965, Parvathaneni said the number of non-permanent members had increased from six to 10 while the five permanent members retained their positions. This changed the ratio of permanent to elected members from 5:6 to 5:10, further strengthening the relative power of the P5, he said.
India has consistently called for expanding both permanent and non-permanent membership categories, warning that efforts focused only on increasing the number of non-permanent members would fall short of meaningful reform.
New Delhi has been advocating Security Council reform for years, arguing that the body, established in 1945, no longer reflects contemporary geopolitical realities. India has maintained that it deserves a permanent seat on the Council.
India is also seeking a non-permanent seat for the 2028-29 term. Elections are scheduled for June next year, when India and Tajikistan will contest the sole seat allocated to the Asia-Pacific Group. India last served on the Council in 2021-22, its eighth term, having previously held seats in 1950-51, 1967-68, 1972-73, 1977-78, 1984-85, 1991-92 and 2011-12.
Parvathaneni also stressed that the veto, currently held by the five permanent members, should be exercised with “great restraint”, particularly on matters concerning international peace and security. He said it should not be used as an instrument of narrow political expediency.
He added that discussions on limiting the veto could not be separated from other aspects of Security Council reform, including membership categories, regional representation, the Council's size and its working methods.
India called for a comprehensive approach to reform, with text-based negotiations beginning at the earliest and proceeding according to clearly defined timelines and milestones.
Parvathaneni further pointed out that the use of veto-like powers extended beyond formal votes by permanent members. According to him, any Security Council member could effectively block presidential statements, press statements and decisions of sanctions committees, where the unwritten rule of consensus allows a single member to obstruct a proposal, often without explanation.
He was referring to the functioning of UNSC sanctions committees, which designate and delist terror outfits and individuals.
The diplomat also criticised the use of consensus as a “disguised, de facto veto” within the Intergovernmental Negotiations process itself. Referring to the UN General Assembly resolution that established the framework for negotiations, he said the guiding principle was the widest possible political acceptance rather than consensus.
“Seventeen cycles later, we have no outcome to show for it,” he said.
India maintained that the Council's credibility, legitimacy and effectiveness could not be restored by addressing the veto alone. Parvathaneni said its structure must reflect present-day realities rather than the outcome of a war fought eight decades ago.

By Steve Goldstein
This handout picture provided by the Iranian presidency shows (R to L) Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian and National Security Council head Mohsen Rezaei during their meeting with Saudi Arabia's Defence Minister, Pakistan's army chief, and Turkey's intelligence chief in Tehran on October 26, 2026.
To the outside world, it's not even clear that Mojtaba Khamenei, the supreme leader of Iran, is alive.
But whether he is or not, Iranian news agencies reported on a meeting Khamenei had with Major General Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of the country's Supreme National Security Council, in which he reportedly called to bring "the current state of neither war nor peace to an end."
To be clear, the remarks indicated that the deal would have to be done on Iran's terms. One clause, according to the Islamic Republic News Agency, is "safeguarding national and regional security by maintaining control over the Strait of Hormuz." That may not fly with the Trump administration that has been escorting tankers, at great cost and peril, through the contested waterway.
The word "nuclear" doesn't come up once in IRNA's reporting. So there's a long way to go between these comments and any sort of U.S.-Iran deal.
That said, Khamenei's desire to end the conflict has not previously been articulated. And it comes after a four-way meeting between Iranian, Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish officials that also was held on Tuesday.

Russia and Ukraine began a localised ceasefire in southern Ukraine overnight under a US-backed agreement to evacuate civilians trapped in the Russian-occupied frontline city of Oleshky.
Russian forces will start clearing mines off the roads leading to the embattled city, where about 2,000 people have been caught in crossfire between the two armies and face severe food shortages.
Buses should take people out of Oleshky on Thursday morning, while humanitarian aid will be brought in for residents who decline to leave.
The ceasefire, which will last until November 1, is “the most significant de-escalation since 2022”, one of Ukraine’s chief negotiators, David Arakhamia, wrote on social media.
Arakhamia and the White House said first lady Melania Trump helped secure the agreement, which was announced on October 23 after weeks of campaigning by Kyiv. Pope Leo XIV had called Russian President Vladimir Putin on October 16 to push for the ceasefire.
Melania Trump said on Tuesday the ceasefire had been “expanded” to the entire Kherson region.
Ukrainian authorities had said on Monday that the ceasefire would apply to the Kherson region as a whole and confirmed that both sides were adhering to it on Tuesday afternoon.
The deal came during a push to renew peace talks to end the conflict in Ukraine. US President Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff met Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Oslo last week before travelling to St Petersburg for talks with Putin.
Putin on Tuesday held a phone call with the leaders of Norway and Finland, who hosted the Oslo talks and called on the Russian leader to end the war. Ukraine and Russia have agreed to resume peace talks in Abu Dhabi in coming days.
Oleshky, a quiet city on the Dnipro River with a population of about 24,000 before Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion, has been cut off from the rest of the region by drone strikes and mines, making it nearly impossible for food and medicine to reach it. Most of the city does not have electricity, heating or water.
Residents “are starving, surviving on leftover garden vegetables, preserves and even snails”, Ukrainian foreign minister Andriy Sybiha wrote on X this month.
People who agreed to leave would be taken to Crimea or Russia before they were able to return to Ukraine, people with knowledge of the discussions told the FT.
“Russia will do everything it can to de-mine in such a way that these people go towards Russia and remain there,” Zelenskyy warned in an interview on Ukrainian television on Sunday. “Our people and society need to be prepared for how they will sell it: ‘Look, we see thousands of people who really want to go to Russia, and those fascists were shelling them.’”
Zelenskyy accused Russia of blocking and mining the road out of Oleshky, while Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov has alleged that Ukrainian forces had hindered deliveries of food and medicine.
Ukrainian forces have increasingly targeted Russian supply lines in southern Ukraine in what then-defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov called a “logistics lockdown” in May. The intensified drone strikes aimed to cut off Crimea and weaken Russian frontline units.
Moscow took control of Oleshky in the early days of the invasion, and the city turned into a frontline position following the Russian retreat in autumn 2022. The Russian destruction of the Kakhovka Dam in 2023 triggered a massive flood that devastated the city and probably killed hundreds of residents, an Associated Press investigation found.
One local, who fled the city in 2023, said residents had told him the situation turned critical a year ago, as it became increasingly deadly for people to drive out of the city. A humanitarian volunteer, who had been helping people flee, died in January when his vehicle hit a mine hidden by snow.
By summer this year, drone footage of the thoroughfare heading out of Oleshky showed a road littered with charred vehicles.
Russian drone units on the Dnipro have repeatedly hit civilians, including ambulances and pedestrians, in nearby Kherson and other settlements. A UN commission concluded last year the attacks “suggest a co-ordinated state policy, on the part of the Russian authorities, to force the population of Kherson Province to leave the area”. The commission said the attacks “amount to crimes against humanity”.
Localised ceasefires have been rare and fraught with tension since 2022. A corridor in the Zaporizhzhia region allowed civilians to cross the frontline during the first months of the full-scale invasion but was closed after a Russian missile strike on a civilian convoy killed 32 people in September 2022.
Several localised ceasefires have been brokered by the International Atomic Energy Agency to repair infrastructure serving the Russian-controlled Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant.
Separately, a Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv killed one person and injured 15 overnight, Ukraine’s state emergency service reported on Tuesday. Missiles damaged a university building, a metro station and a bridge in the capital.

articles.summary: U.S. Expert Warns Lee Jae Myung's Conciliatory Policy Risks War  조선일보
articles.full_text:
A U.S. foreign and security policy expert has criticized President Lee Jae Myung’s conciliatory approach toward North Korea, arguing that it has instead provoked Pyongyang’s provocations and heightened the risk of war on the Korean Peninsula. The expert also claimed that U.S. President Donald Trump’s decision to scale down joint South Korea-U.S. military drills and push for a summit with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un has sent the wrong signal to North Korea.
Dan Blumenthal, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute (AEI), wrote in a September 27 op-ed for The Washington Post (WP) titled ‘The Korean Peninsula Is an Economic Powder Keg. If It Explodes, It Could Cost Trillions of Dollars’ that “President Lee Jae Myung’s approach to North Korea has also increased the likelihood of conflict.”
Blumenthal, an East Asia security expert, served as a senior official overseeing China, Taiwan, and Mongolia at the U.S. Department of Defense during the George W. Bush administration (2001–2004) and was a member of the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission under the U.S. Congress from 2006 to 2012. He currently researches Chinese and East Asian security issues at AEI, a leading conservative U.S. think tank.
He pointed out that President Lee halted anti-North Korea propaganda broadcasts last year, cracked down on leaflet campaigns sending information into North Korea, and reduced support for North Korean human rights. Blumenthal also criticized Lee’s proposal to ease sanctions on North Korea in exchange for freezing its nuclear weapons and intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) development. “Kim Jong-un responded to these one-sided concessions by calling South Korea ‘the most hostile enemy,’” Blumenthal wrote.
He specifically cited the September 21 explosion of a North Korean landmine in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) that injured three South Korean soldiers as an example of the flaws in Lee’s policy. “The September 21 landmine explosion in the DMZ, which injured three South Korean soldiers, demonstrates the dangers of responding to provocations with appeasement,” Blumenthal argued. He added that the following day, President Lee requested President Trump to help restart dialogue with Kim Jong-un.
Blumenthal criticized Lee for describing the landmine incident as an “unfortunate accident” despite the U.N. Command ruling it a violation of the Korean War armistice and the South Korean Defense Minister assigning responsibility to North Korea. He also noted that North Korea launched a mid-range ballistic missile capable of flying over 700 km less than two weeks after the explosion. Blumenthal argued that South Korea’s conciliatory response to North Korea’s military provocations could embolden Kim Jong-un rather than deter him.
Blumenthal extended his criticism to the Trump administration’s North Korea policy. He mentioned that in March, the U.S. Department of Defense relocated parts of the Patriot and THAAD (Terminal High Altitude Area Defense) systems deployed in South Korea to the Middle East to support the war in Iran. He also criticized Trump for scaling down the annual South Korea-U.S. joint military drills in August, stating that the exercises sent “inappropriate and hostile” signals, while claiming to maintain a good relationship with Kim Jong-un. “If Kim Jong-un believes that South Korea and the U.S. will respond jointly, he is less likely to attack South Korea,” Blumenthal said. “However, Washington and Seoul are giving him reasons to doubt their shared resolve.”
Blumenthal firmly opposed Trump’s hope to hold a summit with Kim Jong-un within this year. “Trump hopes to meet Kim Jong-un this year, perhaps as early as November,” he said. “That would be a mistake.” He argued that any measures to elevate Kim Jong-un’s status while his strategic position is improving would only make him more dangerous.
Blumenthal noted that North Korea is in a stronger position than at any other time since the Cold War, having deployed approximately 14,000 troops to Russia to gain combat experience. In return, Russia has reportedly provided North Korea with air defense and electronic warfare capabilities and is considering transferring more advanced military technology. He also analyzed that China has de facto tolerated North Korea’s nuclear status while continuing economic support, citing Chinese President Xi Jinping’s omission of North Korea’s nuclear program during his June visit to Pyongyang.
In this context, Blumenthal raised the possibility that Kim Jong-un could escalate provocations to trigger a military response from South Korea and the U.S. or attack South Korea if a war breaks out between China and Taiwan. He argued that if China faces disadvantages in a war with Taiwan, it might pressure North Korea to open a second front to divert U.S. military forces. Blumenthal warned that an actual war on the Korean Peninsula would cause catastrophic damage not only to human lives but also to the global economy.
He pointed out that Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix supply approximately two-thirds of the advanced memory semiconductors needed for AI accelerators, and South Korea’s major semiconductor production facilities, including the world’s largest, are within North Korea’s attack range. He analyzed that since state-of-the-art semiconductor facilities require hundreds of billions of dollars to build and years to reach normal production capacity, it would be virtually impossible for other countries to replace South Korea’s production facilities in the short term if they were destroyed.
Blumenthal predicted that a war on the Korean Peninsula would cause computer and smartphone prices to skyrocket, halt global electronics production, and sharply slow data center construction. Citing a 2024 Bloomberg analysis, he warned that the global economy could suffer losses exceeding 4 trillion dollars in the first year of a Korean Peninsula war, equivalent to approximately 3.5% of the world’s GDP. “The risk of conflict is growing, and the threat to the international economy is serious,” Blumenthal argued. “Trump and Lee Jae Myung must restore deterrence rather than reward Kim Jong-un’s aggressive actions to avoid a strategic and economic disaster.”

articles.full_text:
ROME (AP) — Pope Leo XIV on Tuesday denounced any religious justification for wars raging around the world, saying “there is no such thing as a holy war.”
“Only peace is holy,” Leo said in a video-message to a gathering of religious leaders in the Italian hilltop town of Assisi.
The American pope was supposed to have presided over the gathering in person, but had to cancel his participation as he recovers from Oct. 13 lung cancer surgery.
Instead, Leo sent a videotaped message that was broadcast to the delegates, who included the Archbishop of Canterbury Sarah Mullally, spiritual leader of the worldwide Anglican Communion, as well as Muslim, Buddhist and other Christian leaders.
They were in Assisi, the birthplace of the peace-loving St. Francis, to mark the 40th anniversary of a landmark interfaith peace meeting called by St. John Paul II. That encounter, controversial at the time because it featured leaders of different faiths praying together, spawned a movement of interreligious peace appeals and gatherings.
In his message, the American pope denounced the “troubling revival of war as an instrument of international politics” and its religious justifications by leaders.
“Precisely in these times marked by a culture of power, there is a need to cultivate the spirit of Assisi,” he said. “War can never be waged in the name of God,” he said. “We must rebuild peace everywhere, not prepare for more wars.”
Leaders use religion to justify war
Russia’s Orthodox Church has justified Russia’s invasion of Ukraine as a “holy war” against a Western world it considers has fallen into evil.
Leaders on all sides of the Iran war have used religion to justify their actions. U.S. officials, especially Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, have invoked their Christian faith to cast the war as a Christian nation trying to vanquish its foes with military might.
Leo has consistently rejected such justifications as a perversion of religion itself, most stridently in his first encyclical “Magnificent Humanity” in which he said fighting in the name of religion “means attacking religion itself.”
Vatican brings new aid to Ukraine
The Assisi gathering came as the Vatican is accelerating its humanitarian efforts for Ukraine following the entry into effect of a localized cease-fire in the devastated southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky. The pope’s chief almsgiver, Monsignor Luis Marín de San Martín, on Tuesday began a three-day visit to Ukraine and was bringing several trucks worth of winter clothes, blankets and food to Kyiv for distribution.
Marín de San Martín was planning to visit Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro and Fastiv, Vatican News said.
Leo had called for a cease-fire and the delivery of food and medicine in Oleshky, and the safe and voluntary evacuation of its people during an Oct. 16 phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, which the pontiff initiated from the hospital where he was recovering from surgery.
Leo followed up three days later, back at the Vatican, with a call to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. According to the Vatican, Leo noted his appeal for a cease-fire to Putin and “expressed the hope that cooperation between both parties will allow for the delivery of food and medical aid, and for the voluntary and safe evacuation of the civilian population.”
The White House said the cease-fire in Oleshky was secured by first lady Melania Trump. Asked Tuesday, the Vatican foreign minister, Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher, said the Vatican wasn’t aware of the first lady’s role but also dismissed any polemics over who was ultimately responsible.
“I think it’s one of those situations in which it doesn’t matter who actually brought it about or who takes the credit, it’s the fact that hopefully it is real, it will last, it will allow for evacuation and it will allow the arrival of humanitarian aid to help the people who are left behind.”
The Vatican initiatives took place after Italian Cardinal Matteo Zuppi, the papal envoy for the Ukraine-Russia war, finished his third mission to Moscow on Sept. 30 and the first under Leo’s pontificate. Zuppi has focused his initiatives on humanitarian issues, especially reuniting Ukrainian children taken by Russia with their families, and Gallagher said for now neither Russia nor Ukraine wants the Holy See to take on a greater mediation or facilitation role.

Jon Stewart skewered President Donald Trump over his repeated remarks about “big butts” in the lead-up to the midterm elections.
During at least four rallies this month, the 80-year-old president has marveled at Ohio Senator John Husted’s behind, declaring in Kentucky: “I examined his a**.” He gave the same treatment to Nicki Minaj one week later in Michigan, stating that the pro-Trump rapper has “one hell of a beautiful a**.”
“Voters are for some reason fixated on the economy, cost of living, the war in Iran,” Stewart said on Monday’s episode of The Daily Show. “Donald Trump is actually back out there on the campaign trail to make his closing arguments. The comedian then cut to a montage of Trump discussing derrieres.

“By the way, don’t feel left out, ladies. Trump’s got plenty of ogle left for you,” the comedian continued.

articles.title: CISA Warns Hackers Are Exploiting PHP2Shell Flaws to Target Web Servers - Cyber Press
articles.summary: CISA Warns Hackers Are Exploiting PHP2Shell Flaws to Target Web Servers  Cyber Press
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added two critical PHP vulnerabilities, collectively tracked in reporting as “PHP2Shell,” to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after evidence indicated active exploitation against web-facing systems.
The flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, affect PHP and can enable unauthenticated remote code execution, creating a serious risk for organizations operating exposed web servers.
CVE-2026-109618 is described as an out-of-memory corruption vulnerability in PHP that may allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code remotely.
CISA Warns of PHP2Shell Flaws
CVE-2026-109619 is a stale internal request-state vulnerability that can also result in unauthenticated remote code execution.
Both issues fall under memory-safety and state-management weakness categories, including CWE-416, CWE-755, CWE-824, CWE-1325, and CWE-1419.
CISA added the vulnerabilities to its catalog on October 26, 2026, with a remediation deadline of October 29, 2026, reflecting the agency’s assessment of their urgency.
CISA’s entry does not identify a confirmed ransomware campaign tied to either vulnerability, but it marks forensic triage as required under Binding Operational Directive 26-04.
PHP is widely deployed across internet-facing websites, content-management systems, application programming interfaces, and enterprise web applications.
A remotely exploitable flaw in the PHP runtime can therefore create a broad attack surface, especially when vulnerable installations process attacker-controlled requests.
Successful exploitation could allow threat actors to run commands on a server, deploy web shells, steal application credentials, access databases, or establish a foothold for lateral movement.
The use of “unauthenticated” in the vulnerability descriptions is particularly significant. Attackers may not need legitimate credentials or prior access to target an affected system if a reachable PHP service processes the malicious input needed to trigger the flaw.
Treat internet-exposed systems as the highest-priority assets because automated scanning and opportunistic exploitation commonly follow public disclosure of severe remote-code-execution bugs.
CISA directed affected organizations to apply mitigations according to vendor guidance and comply with the risk-based patching requirements in BOD 26-04. When mitigation is unavailable, the agency advises organizations to stop using the affected product.
The directive also requires stakeholders to evaluate whether each affected asset is exposed to the internet and to follow applicable cloud-service remediation guidance.
Security teams should begin by identifying PHP deployments across production, development, cloud, and third-party-hosted environments.
Administrators should verify installed versions, review vendor advisories for fixed releases and mitigations, and prioritize systems that accept public web traffic.
Organizations should also inspect web-server, PHP, endpoint, and authentication logs for suspicious activity preceding patching, since CISA has designated forensic triage as necessary for both vulnerabilities.
Defenders should look for unexpected processes spawned by web-server accounts, abnormal PHP child processes, newly written files in web-accessible directories, unfamiliar scheduled tasks, altered application configuration files, and unusual outbound network connections.
If there are signs of compromise, affected organizations should preserve relevant logs and system artifacts before rebuilding or rotating credentials.
Because PHP2Shell exploitation can lead to server-level code execution, patching alone may not be enough for systems exposed before remediation.
Incident responders should confirm that no persistence mechanisms, web shells, stolen secrets, or unauthorized accounts remain after updating the vulnerable PHP software.

articles.title: EU wants capitals to adjust to warming of 3°C - Euronews.com
articles.summary: EU wants capitals to adjust to warming of 3°C  Euronews.comEU tells countries to make plans to cope with 3C of global warming  Financial TimesEEA welcomes the Climate Resilience Framework and launches new tools to help Europe prepare  European Environment Agency (EEA)EU prepares for a grim future with new climate-proofing law  POLITICO.euNature deserves a stronger role in EU Climate Resilience Law  BirdLife International
articles.full_text:
As Brussels warns that Europe must prepare for increasingly extreme weather, new EU rules will require governments to clarify who is responsible for climate preparedness – but no new funding is being offered to help households adapt.
The European Commission will unveil new climate rules on Tuesday requiring EU governments to clarify who is responsible for protecting citizens from climate disasters, Climate Action Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra told Euronews.
The move comes as Brussels warns that Europe must prepare for increasingly extreme weather, including scenarios involving 3°C of global warming by 2100.
Hoekstra warned that the world is heading towards a temporary or potentially prolonged overshoot of the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C warming limit, making it essential for governments to prepare for more extreme heat and climate disasters, even if efforts to cut emissions succeed.
“It is up to member states to decide where they want to put that responsibility. But what we do make mandatory is that they do have to appoint and articulate where the responsibility is going to lie,” Hoekstra said.
While the EU continues to pursue emissions reductions, the costs of adapting to a hotter world are becoming harder to ignore, from rebuilding after wildfires and floods to protecting homes, roads and public infrastructure.
The Dutch Commissioner estimated the economic damage from this summer's extreme weather at more than €100 billion.
Asked what a 3°C rise above pre-industrial temperatures could mean for Europeans, Hoekstra pointed to heat plans for cities and the need to prepare infrastructure for a hotter future, rather than relying on historical weather patterns.
The reference trajectory is based on scientific research, including work by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change and advanced European climate modeling, he said.
The Commission's projections envisage 2°C of global warming by 2050 and 3°C by 2100 for Europe, reflecting Brussels' assessment that Europe is warming roughly twice as fast as the global average.
The trajectory is intended to be translated into national and local risk assessments, taking account of the uneven distribution of climate impacts.
“Even if we get all of this right, we have no way to avoid more summers than the one we saw last year,” the Commissioner said, arguing that readiness, resilience and preparedness must become the priority alongside emissions cuts.
The proposed legislation would require EU countries to specify whether national, regional or local authorities are responsible for preparing for climate disasters.
Governments would retain flexibility over how they allocate responsibilities, but would have to specify who is accountable — an attempt to prevent political disputes over who failed to prepare when floods or wildfires destroy homes.
The Commission also wants climate scenarios to be considered when planning new roads, bridges and neighbourhoods, recognising that infrastructure designed for past weather conditions may no longer be fit for purpose.
"We want to introduce a culture of preparedness and resilience by design, rather than dealing with the damages in the aftermath, which is often very ad hoc and doesn't always build back better," a senior Commission official said on Monday on condition of anonymity.
No new money
However, the question of how to pay for climate adaptation remains unresolved.
No new financial commitment to household support is expected from the Commission's climate resilience strategy, despite concerns that ordinary citizens may struggle to afford the investments needed to adapt.
Hoekstra pointed to the Commission's proposal to devote 35% of the EU budget to climate and nature.
But the strategy's effectiveness will depend partly on the outcome of ongoing negotiations over the EU's next multiannual budget, with climate spending competing against priorities such as defence, security, competitiveness and agricultural support.
The Commission is also counting on the recently announced €30 billion from the European Investment Bank for climate adaptation through 2030.
Nonetheless, the lack of new funding is a potential weakness in the Commission's ambition.
The Commissioner argued that preventive investment is economically worth it but did not announce a new household support scheme or explain how the EU would ensure that lower-income households could afford necessary improvements.
In an attempt to fill the bloc's climate protection gap, Brussels wants to work with the insurance sector, as Commissioner Hoekstra pointed out that many areas in Europe are underinsured against climate disasters.
According to the senior Commission official, only around 25% of assets exposed to climate impacts are insured, leaving governments and property owners vulnerable to substantial losses.
“The fact that so many areas are underinsured” is one of the issues the Commission will examine, Hoekstra said.
The strategy could therefore expose another fault line between Brussels' climate ambitions and the cost-of-living pressures facing European voters.

New EU-proposed rules will require countries to make plans to adapt to a 3C rise in global temperatures from pre-industrial levels, as its climate chief warned efforts to cut emissions were “no longer nearly good enough”.
The world is on course for a 2.8C rise in the average temperature since the industrial era by 2100 under current international government policies, and this would be the first legal proposal to prepare member states for that eventuality when making policies and investments.
It will also require countries to designate the bodies responsible for managing climate risks in different areas of the economy, according to a draft proposal seen by the FT.
“Even if we do everything right today in the domain of mitigation, it will not be enough to get our citizens out of harm’s way,” EU climate commissioner Wopke Hoekstra told the FT. “Last summer simply proved that alone is no longer nearly good enough.”
High temperatures contributed to about 50,000 deaths across the continent in summer this year, far exceeding the previous record of 29,000 heat-related deaths in the summer of 2022.
The latest UN report released Tuesday found that the climate commitments made by 154 countries who signed up to the Paris accord to limit climate change could reduce global greenhouse gas emissions by only 6 per cent by 2035 — or a tenth of the 60 per cent cut from 2019 levels which is needed to keep warming to 1.5C.
To stay below 2C, emissions would need to fall by 37 per cent by 2035, scientists estimate. The report by the UN climate change body on the so-called nationally determined contributions, received from January 2024 to August 2026, covered 71 per cent of global emissions.
The latest EU proposal comes as part of a climate resilience framework to ensure Europe adapts to rising temperatures. The continent is warming at about twice the global average, partly as a result of proximity to the melting Arctic.
The framework marks a change of focus for the European Commission as the rise in temperatures puts more need to turn to efforts to adapt to the damage caused by climate change as well as lowering emissions.
Some climate campaigners argue the focus on adapting to higher temperatures risks diverting resources from action to cut greenhouse gas emissions.
The latest policy move comes a few weeks ahead of the COP31 climate summit in Turkey, where Europe is expected to take the lead in pressing other nations to increase climate action despite backsliding on some of its own proposals.
The Commission anticipates the EU needs to spend €70bn a year on adaptation until 2050. But the adaptation proposal will not come with any finance — such as a levy on fossil fuel companies being pushed by Spain.
Funding for measures that would deal with action to cut emissions will be dependent on ongoing negotiations over the EU’s long-term budget.
The proposal will also fall short of calls by Madrid and others to place a legally-binding “duty” for authorities to ensure public investments take climate risks into account.
A person familiar with the discussion said the “duty” requirement had been removed during the drafting process over concerns this could trigger legal repercussions.
However, Hoekstra insisted a legal proposal to take into account the 3C temperature rise by 2100 and the measures on “risk ownership” would have “teeth” to ensure Europe reacts more quickly to climate change consequences.
“Clarity upfront on who should do what, who is responsible, is hugely important,” he said, highlighting the summer heatwaves and recent floods in Valencia. “Europe will see many more floods, many more heatwaves and many more wildfires.”

A localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine around the occupied city of Oleshky that first lady Melania Trump helped to broker has now gone into effect, officials on both sides said Tuesday.
Dmytro Lubinets, the Ukrainian parliament commissioner for human rights, said on X that the ceasefire went into effect at 3:00 a.m. Kyiv time Tuesday.
Russia’s defense ministry said on Telegram it stopped shelling in the direction of Oleshky at the same time Tuesday.
The pause in fighting is intended to allow for the evacuation of elderly residents and the entry of urgently needed humanitarian aid to the frontline city, which has been occupied by Russia since the first days of the full-scale invasion in 2022. Ukrainian authorities have said about 1,700 people remain in Oleshky.
Lubinets said the ceasefire is “part of a humanitarian mission being carried out with the mediation and coordination of US First Lady Melania Trump, in cooperation with Yana Lantratova, Russia’s Commissioner for Human Rights.”
The first lady announced Tuesday that the ceasefire area had expanded “beyond Oleshky, within the Kherson Region, to provide safe passage for the humanitarian convoys.” She said that the expanded region was “confirmed” by Russian official General Valery Vasilyevich (Gerasimov), and that it went into effect two days earlier than she had previously announced in order “to protect the safety of civilians and to facilitate the delivery of critical humanitarian aid.”
The Office of the Ukrainian Ombudsman, which Lubinets heads, later confirmed that the ceasefire was in effect throughout the Kherson region.
“We’ve been working to resolve the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky since late February 2026. Things really started moving in September — thanks to Melania Trump. The US side is monitoring how each party is fulfilling its commitments,” Lubinets said on Ukrainian TV channel 1+1.
“As soon as the road is cleared and the cargo is delivered, representatives from all three countries will be there. Anyone who wants to travel to Ukraine will be able to do so,” he added.
The ceasefire is expected to remain in place until November 1, according to Ukrainian MP Davyd Arakhamia, who is also a key peace negotiator.
Across the Dnipro river from Oleshky in the city of Kherson – the largest Ukrainian city on the front line, which has endured brutal attacks on civilians and infrastructure due to its unique tactical position – residents are relieved.
But they know this reprieve cannot last.
“People are happy, but everyone’s afraid that after this ceasefire, they’ll give us such a beating that it’ll be beyond belief,” Zhanna Yakovleva, who lives in Kherson, told CNN on Tuesday.
“That’s the reality, unfortunately.”
Two civilians have been killed in the Kherson region since October 20, and a further 38 have sustained injuries – including six children.
Many, like Yakovleva, are living with friends and relatives because their homes have been damaged or destroyed.
Amid the temporary calm, people have taken to the streets to check on those houses and apartments, Yakovleva said, something they’ve been unable to do because of relentless Russian drone strikes.
Yakovleva described Kherson, which was the first major city to fall under Russian occupation in 2022 and was liberated by Ukraine later that year, as quiet – for the first time since its de-occupation.
Posting on Telegram, Arakhamia said it was “the most extensive ceasefire to date… along the largest section of the front line in southern Ukraine.”
“This is the largest de-escalation effort since 2022,” he added.
By late Tuesday afternoon local time, Lubinets confirmed that both Ukraine and Russia were “adhering” to the ceasefire in the designated areas.
Russian Human Rights Commissioner Lantratova also said that no violations of the ceasefire had been recorded on either side, adding: “It is very important that the agreements reached continue to be observed.”
Elsewhere, fighting continued.
A 46-year-old woman was killed and more than a dozen people were injured in an attack on Kyiv, which also damaged a bridge, Ukraine’s Emergency Service said.
Russia’s military said it carried out a “massive strike” targeting Ukrainian military facilities, a logistics center in Kharkiv, and transport infrastructure in Kyiv. It also said it intercepted and destroyed 222 Ukrainian drones over its territory.
How did Melania Trump broker the ceasefire?
The first lady announced Friday she had worked with Ukrainian and Russian leadership to secure the localized ceasefire as the “exclusive intermediary.”
“The people of Oleshky have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks,” Melania Trump said in a statement Friday.
“Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require,” she added.
“Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine.”
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Saturday Kyiv had been working to negotiate this deal for “some time.” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov credited Trump for her “significant contribution.”
Donald Trump praised his wife’s efforts on Friday, saying “they contacted both sides, and both sides wanted to do it.” He said that her focus remains on helping the children impacted by the war.
Pope Leo also discussed the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky on an October 16 phone call with Putin while in the hospital recovering from lung cancer surgery, according to the Vatican.
The first lady’s office said last week that the circumstances of Oleshky came to her attention during a private discussion at the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York in September.
This story has been updated with additional information.
Daria Tarasova-Markina, Anna Chernova, Kosta Gak and Betsy Klein contributed reporting.

articles.summary: Exclusive: UK leans towards backing UAE's Lana Nusseibeh for UN secretary-general  Middle East EyeRights monitors raise concerns over senior UAE diplomat bid for next UN boss  ReutersThe UAE has so much blood on its hands in Sudan. For its nominee to lead the UN would be an outrage | Nesrine Malik  The GuardianIsrael’s Danon Praises UAE’s Nusseibeh But Stops Short Of Backing Her UN Bid  i24NEWSWho is Lana Nusseibeh, the UAE diplomat hoping to become the ne...
articles.full_text:
The United Kingdom is leaning towards backing Emirati diplomat Lana Nusseibeh as secretary-general of the United Nations, Middle East Eye can reveal.
Nusseibeh's candidacy has drawn controversy over the United Arab Emirates' role in Sudan’s civil war, where it is accused of supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, whose mass killings UN investigators say bear the “hallmarks of genocide”. The UAE denies the allegations.
Her candidacy has also drawn criticism over the UAE's close ties with Israel.
Numerous sources close to the British government told Middle East Eye the UK - a permanent member of the UN - is leaning towards supporting Nusseibeh's candidacy for the role, although a final decision has not yet been made.
A British Foreign Office spokesperson told MEE: "The UK’s priority is to find the candidate best equipped to lead the UN in tackling our shared global challenges.
"Our focus is on the merit of the candidates to secure the most qualified candidate for the next UN secretary-general. We will not be publicly commenting on individual candidates."
The UK supporting Nusseibeh could be perceived as smoothening Prime Minister Andy Burnham's relationship with Abu Dhabi after a major row in Britain over Manchester City Football Club, owned by Emirati royal and vice-president Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nayhan.
The club was found last month to have breached 114 Premier League financial rules by disguising more than £830m ($1.1bn) in illicit funding.
Manchester City denies the claims and Emirati officials have since reportedly threatened to cancel investments in Britain over "the Premier League’s actions".
Multiple sources said that if the UK backs Nusseibeh as UN secretary-general, it might win the country some goodwill with the UAE at a time when relations are fraught.
If selected Nusseibeh, 48, would be the first woman to lead the UN and its second Arab secretary-general, after Egypt's Boutros Boutros-Ghali.
Her entry into the race last week followed six informal straw polls in which no candidate secured the backing of the five veto-wielding permanent members of the UN: Britain, the US, Russia, China and France.
The current secretary-general, Antonio Guterres, will end his term in December. The council must agree a candidate for the 193-member General Assembly to approve, but it remains unclear whether it will do so before then.
Controversial record
Born in 1978, Nusseibeh worked as a Unesco consultant and an analyst at the Gulf Research Centre before becoming founding director of the UAE foreign ministry's policy planning department.
She became the UAE's first female permanent representative to the UN in 2013 and served until 2024, during which time she was a vice-president of the General Assembly, president of the UN Women executive board and twice president of the Security Council.
Nusseibeh is of Palestinian heritage and her family hails from Jerusalem. Her grandfather, Anwar Nusseibeh, was a prominent Palestinian politician who held ministerial posts in Jordan's government when it controlled the West Bank and East Jerusalem, and served as Jordan's ambassador to Britain.
Colin Shindler, an emeritus professor of Israeli studies at Soas who taught her when she was a student at that university, wrote in a 2020 Jewish Chronicle column that she had completed a master's in Israeli studies.
He said she'd wrote some "wonderfully insightful and incisive essays on Zionism and Israeli history", and described her as "instrumental" in the normalisation deal, known as the Abraham Accords.
In September 2025, as Israel weighed annexing parts of the occupied West Bank, Nusseibeh said the UAE had always seen the accords as a way to support Palestinians and urged the Israeli government to suspend its plans.
"I am standing to be secretary-general because I believe this is a moment to act with greater urgency: to act earlier, bring people together across difference, and drive the work forward until it produces concrete results," she said in a statement launching her campaign last week.
Sudan atrocities
On Monday, the UK announced it was sanctioning 15 senior commanders from both the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) in Sudan for "suspected atrocities, including conflict-related sexual violence".
This comes a year after the RSF massacred civilians in Sudan's Al Fasher. British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said: "A year on from the atrocities in El Fasher, UK-funded investigations have shown that rape and starvation are still being weaponised against the people of Sudan.
"These are crimes against our humanity - the perpetrators must be held accountable and support from all external backers to the warring parties must end."
UN experts and rights groups have concluded in several authoritative reports that the RSF has committed genocide and other international crimes against non-Arab communities in Darfur.
There is widespread public evidence, including extensive reporting by MEE, linking the UAE with the supply of arms and other goods to the RSF, although the Emirati government, including Nusseibeh, have repeatedly denied this.

Human Rights Panel Says  The New York TimesGaza ceasefire has not stopped Israel from committing genocide, UN-commissioned experts say  AP NewsUN Inquiry Finds Israel Committed Crimes Against Humanity in West Bank  Haaretz'Legitimazes Jihad': Foreign Ministry slams UN report accusing Israel of genocide&nbsp...
articles.full_text:
A United Nations commission of inquiry has accused Israel of committing crimes against humanity in the occupied West Bank, including extermination, torture and rape, while also continuing “to commit genocide in Gaza” despite a ceasefire brokered by the United States.
The report, published on Monday by the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, examined killings and physical and mental harm inflicted by state actors from October 7, 2023, through September of this year.
It was released the day before Israel’s general election.
The commission found that the situation in the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967, had “deteriorated gravely” since the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on October 7, 2023.
It said Israeli military operations, reinforced by sustained violence by settlers, amounted to a “widespread and systematic attack” on civilians, and that Israeli authorities “intended to collectively punish” residents of the occupied West Bank for the Hamas-led attack on Israel.
“The Israeli authorities and forces have committed the crimes against humanity of extermination, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence in the West Bank, as well as persecution based on intersecting discriminatory grounds, with nationality, race and ethnicity at its core,” the report said.
Extermination
The commission also found a sharp rise in deaths from air strikes in the territory.
Six Palestinians were killed in air attacks in the occupied West Bank from 2008 to October 6, 2023, it said, compared with 254 from October 7, 2023, to September 30, 2026.
“The intentional killing and injuring of Palestinian civilians and destruction of homes in the West Bank combined with Israel’s persistent denial of responsibility form part of a broader strategy to exterminate and displace Palestinians and impose conditions of life that are unlivable,” said Srinivasan Muralidhar, the commission’s chair.
“Meanwhile, Israel’s expansion of territorial control in Gaza continues to result in the killing and harming of Palestinian civilians who approach or cross” the so-called Yellow Line that demarcates Israeli-controlled areas in the enclave, he said.
Israel’s mission in Geneva called the report part of the commission’s “misinformation campaign to demonize the State of Israel and portray its very existence as criminal”.
“The international community must reject these distortions, repudiate the commission’s findings and demand its immediate dissolution,” the mission said in a statement.
Continued genocide
The commission, which does not speak for the UN as a whole, first concluded in September 2025 that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza during the war that followed the October 7 attacks. Israel has flatly rejected the UN commission’s finding.
In its new report, the commission said Israeli forces had continued to commit “genocidal acts” against Palestinians in Gaza despite the ceasefire brokered by the US last October, with attacks intended to “destroy the Palestinian people, in whole or in part”.
At least five Palestinians, including a seven-year-old girl, were killed in Israeli air attacks across Gaza on Monday, according to medical officials there. The Gaza Health Ministry says at least 74,500 people have been killed in the genocidal war, which has displaced nearly all of the territory’s population.
The report also examined abuses by Palestinian security forces. It found that the Palestinian Authority had targeted people who voiced dissent, and that the killing and wounding of journalists and human rights defenders had steadily narrowed space for civil society.
The three-member commission was established by the UN Human Rights Council in 2021.
Navi Pillay, a former South African High Court judge who led it until last November, won the Nobel Peace Prize this month.
West Bank lockdown
The report was released as Israeli forces carried out a crackdown in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron after a shooting near the city last week. Israel imposed a lockdown on Hebron on Friday, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced plans to extend it across the entire West Bank.
Later on Monday, Volker Turk, the UN high commissioner for human rights, condemned the Hebron operation. He said threats to empty and erase neighbourhoods raised “serious concerns of ethnic cleansing”.
According to Turk, the lockdown had already forcibly displaced more than 2,000 Palestinians, led to the demolition of homes and prevented residents from moving freely.
“The sweeping steps taken raise grave concerns of unnecessary and disproportionate use of force – which must end,” he said.
“The Israeli lockdown is confining many to their homes and their immediate neighbourhoods. Declarations by senior Israeli government officials indicate that the measures implemented are punitive in nature and designed to instil fear. This is unacceptable,” Turk added.
Some Israeli ministers have previously called for the occupied West Bank and Gaza to be ethnically cleansed.
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich told Ynet News last month that Israel should “go to war” in the occupied territory and repeat what it “did in Gaza”. He added that Israeli forces had “cleared out” Palestinian refugee camps in the occupied West Bank.
Turk insisted that people displaced under the clampdown must be allowed to return home and that “Israel must ensure compensation and reparation for unlawful evictions and demolitions”.
“Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law,” he said.

articles.title: Iran hosts regional powers for talks to prevent fresh escalation - Financial Times
articles.summary: Iran hosts regional powers for talks to prevent fresh escalation  Financial TimesIran hosts Saudi Arabia and regional powers as fears grow of return to war  CNNTehran summit divides Iranian hardliners over Yemen and US talks  Iran InternationalIran, Saudi, Turkiye and Pakistan agree to more talks amid Houthi attacks  Al JazeeraSaudi defence pact countries push for peace in Tehran as Houthis launch more attacks  Reuters
articles.full_text:
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Monday to step up efforts to prevent a new round of hostilities in the US-Israeli war with Iran.
The talks in Tehran are part of a flurry of diplomacy to push for an interim deal, amid fears that a new round of the war could erupt after next week’s midterm elections in the US. The meeting is the first between the members of the so-called Mecca mutual defence agreement as a group with Iran.
Oil prices, which have been trading at months-long highs because of the heightened tensions in the region, fell back slightly on Monday, with Brent crude, the international benchmark, down under $116 a barrel in early afternoon trading in London. 
Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said Saudi defence minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani military chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and Turkey’s intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin attended the talks. Pezeshkian was also present, local media reported.
The Saudi foreign ministry on Monday said the talks aimed to support Qatari and Pakistani mediation efforts and ‘‘de-escalate the current crisis’’. 
“The kingdom emphasises the importance of opening channels for negotiation to prevent a resurgence of military escalation in the region, and to pave the way for an agreement that ends the crisis and secures peace and stability both regionally and globally,” it said in a statement. 
A Qatari delegation was in Tehran on Sunday, “working in co-ordination with the US as part of ongoing efforts to de-escalate regional tensions”, another official said. Munir also visited the republic last week where he held talks with senior Iranian officials.
Qatar and Pakistan have been leading mediation efforts to broker a temporary deal between the US and Iran to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz and get the warring parties back to the negotiating table to resume talks on a final settlement to end the war.
The mediators have been trying to build on a seven-day plan Iran presented at the UN General Assembly last month, under which it would allow shipping through the strait if the US lifts its blockade on Iranian ports and grants Tehran access to some of its frozen assets held overseas. The parties would then restart negotiations on a final deal.
But there have been few signs of progress as Washington and Tehran haggle over the sequencing and the fate of Iran’s 440kg stockpile of highly enriched uranium. The US is insisting that the stockpile, which is enriched close to weapons-grade, be transferred offshore, but Iranian officials publicly reject any such move.
Amid the deadlock, there have been reports that US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu are considering launching a new intense bombing campaign against Iran.
Tehran, meanwhile, has stepped up its attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and vowed a ferocious response if it faces a new bombing campaign, including threats to sabotage undersea cables in the strait and target data centres in the region affiliated with the US and Israel.
Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed the Mecca defence pact in August. They said it was defensive and not targeted at any particular state.
Analysts viewed the agreement as recognition among regional states that they would have to play a greater role in managing relations with Iran in the wake of the US-Israeli war against the Islamic republic.
In speech on Monday at Cambridge university, Oman’s foreign minister Badr Albusaidi said the Gulf states’ goal should be to reach a non-aggression pact with Iran, saying any regional “security architecture that doesn’t include them is inherently unstable”.
He added that the Gulf can “no longer rely upon the co-operation of external partners”, in a thinly veiled reference to its reliance on the US as its prime security guarantor, warning that the “long-term political cost has been too high”.
“This does not mean that external partnerships should be abandoned. It is just that their role in the regional security architecture can no longer be primary,” Albusaidi said.
The talks between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Turkey and Iran come at a critical moment for Riyadh, which faces a deepening crisis as Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have targeted Saudi oil facilities and airports since reigniting a decade-long war in July.
The Houthi attacks caused Saudi Arabia to close Riyadh’s international airport for days and postpone Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s flagship investor conference. 
Riyadh airport gradually began to reopen on Sunday, but the attacks threaten Prince Mohammed’s ambitious development plans and have added to the pressure on global energy prices.
Iran and the US had agreed to a memorandum of understanding in June to reopen the strait and hold talks on a final settlement, including a nuclear deal, but it collapsed after about two weeks, with both sides accusing the other of violating the interim agreement.
The US claims that it is in control of the strait and that oil flows have largely returned to prewar levels. But the vital waterway — through which about a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas passed before the war — remains the main battleground between the foes and energy prices have remained high.
Additional reporting by Ahmed Al Omran in Jeddah and John Paul Rathbone in Istanbul

articles.summary: Putin call pits Finland and Norway against Denmark and Sweden  Euronews.comNorway and Finland hold rare call with Putin to discuss ending war  BBCKyiv hopes for ‘new momentum’ in peace talks after Finnish and Norwegian leaders’ call with Putin – as it happened  The GuardianVladimir Putin lectures Nordic leaders on Russian history  Financial TimesPutin’s peace talks with Nordic leaders divide Europe  The Telegraph
articles.full_text:
Nordic unity broke on Tuesday after the leaders of Finland and Norway held a 90-minute phone call with Vladimir Putin. The Danish and Swedish prime ministers publicly cast doubt on the diplomatic overture.
A rare Nordic split emerged on Tuesday as the leaders of Denmark and Sweden publicly rebuked their counterparts in Finland and Norway for holding a surprise phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The call was the initiative of Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, who recently hosted a round of peace talks in Oslo.
The two leaders urged Putin to end the full-scale invasion of Ukraine and engage in meaningful negotiations to reach a stable, peaceful settlement.
"The discussion was frank and substantive," Stubb said.
"The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussion," he added.
"We stressed the importance of de-escalation," Støre said.
The read-out made clear that Stubb and Støre had spoken to Putin as "leaders of their respective countries and did not speak on behalf of Europe as a whole".
Immediately after, Stubb and Støre phoned Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who thanked them for their "active" support.
But the choreography did little to mitigate the backlash from their neighbours.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen was highly critical, pointing to Russia's escalation against Ukraine as evidence that Moscow is not serious about diplomacy.
The Kremlin's statement released after the call echoed Putin's maximalist tone.
"I am very sceptical about this independent initiative by Norway and Finland. It was not coordinated with any of us," Frederiksen said shortly after the call became public.
"I don't see any signs that Russia desires peace with Europe, neither in the hybrid warfare taking place every single day, nor in Ukraine."
Frederiksen questioned the effectiveness of the overture and drew a parallel with previous go-it-alone attempts, such as when former Hungary Prime Minister Viktor Orbán flew to Moscow to meet with Putin.
"I honestly don't know what they think can be achieved by this," she said.
"We have previously emphasise, with clear backing from the rest of Europe, that when others have gone solo and, for example, travelled to Moscow, it is crucial that we, Europeans, stand together. That is something many of us have fought for."
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson also cast doubt on the initiative, albeit in less harsh terms.
"My impression is that everyone wants peace except Putin. I have pretty low expectations for this kind of (direct) talk," Kristersson said.
"Holding talks that risk splitting the European voice is risky. Now, I'm not saying they have done that at all. I don't yet know what those talks were about," he noted.
"Talks that make Russia more willing to make a decent peace on Ukraine's terms are, of course, good."
In response to the pushback, Støre said Europe should speak with Russia to complement the messages sent by the US administration, which has a different take on the war.
Stubb, Støre, Frederiksen and Kristersson were all in Helsinki, Finland, to attend a leaders-level session of the Nordic Council.
Tuesday's political split is significant given that the four countries always see eye to eye when it comes to Russia's war on Ukraine. They are among the largest bilateral donors to Kyiv and vocal advocates of applying ever-stronger sanctions on Moscow.

articles.summary: Kyiv Ballistic Missile Strike Kills 1, Injures 15 in University Area and Multiple Districts  Kyiv Post1 dead, 15 injured as Russia strikes university and surrounding area in Kyiv, Ukraine says  ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and VideosExplosions heard in Ukraine's Kyiv, Reuters witness says  ReutersUkraine war briefing: Russia strikes Kyiv hours before truce begins in war-ravaged city Oleshky  The GuardianRussian attack on Kyiv kills one person, hit...
articles.full_text:
Russian ballistic missiles struck a university campus and surrounding residential areas in Kyiv late Monday, Oct. 26, killing at least one person and injuring over 10 others, most of them students, as emergency crews searched damaged buildings for people feared trapped under rubble.
The strikes hit the grounds of a university near Kyoto Park and Lisova metro station on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River, damaging student dormitories, residential buildings, and medical facilities.
Kyiv Mayor Vitalii Klitschko said nine of the wounded were hospitalized, including three in serious condition.
President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that further strikes were possible as Russian Shahed drone attacks continued against the capital and other Ukrainian cities.
“There is extensive damage, and there are also reports that people may be trapped under the rubble,” Zelensky wrote on social media.
The Ukrainian leader stressed that the missiles struck crowded civilian areas where, he said, there were no military facilities nearby.
“Unfortunately, there may be more strikes coming,” Zelensky added.
At 8:30 a.m. on Tuesday, the Kyiv City Military Administration (KMVA) reported that the number of casualties had risen to 15.
“Overnight, the enemy attacked the capital with ballistic missiles and [unmanned aerial vehicles] UAVs. As a result of the Russian Federation’s terrorist actions, damage has been recorded in three districts of Kyiv,” the report reads.
Of the 15 casualties, 12 have been hospitalized.
According to the State Emergency Service (DSNS), two fires broke out in non-residential buildings in the Obolonskyi district. Rescuers have extinguished both fires. Two casualties were reported in the district.
In the Holosiivskyi district, the Russian attack damaged transport infrastructure.
University campus and student dormitories damaged
The university affected by the attack was identified as the State University of Trade and Economics (SUTE), located on Kyoto Street in Kyiv’s Desnianskyi district.
The institution, founded in 1946, is one of the capital’s major public universities, with more than 15,000 students across six faculties, according to its official profile.
The university specializes in economics, international trade, finance, law, information technology, and management.
Russia’s ballistic strike landed near a university dormitory, shattering windows and injuring residents, according to Klitschko.
The mayor initially reported that a 20-year-old woman was hospitalized following the strike near the dormitory.
In a subsequent update, Klitschko said most of the 10 people injured in the attack were students living in university accommodation. Nine were taken to hospital.
Ukraine’s State Emergency Service reported damage to university buildings, dormitories and nearby residential properties.
KMVA also reported damage to a school building in the Desnianskyi district.
A paramedic and an emergency medical technician suffered injuries after their ambulance came under fire in the Desnianskyi district, according to the mayor. Their injuries were not considered critical.
A strike near Lisova metro station also set a private vehicle on fire, while nearby residential infrastructure sustained damage.
In the Dniprovskyi district, a three-story non-residential building was partially destroyed, with emergency workers discovering the body of one person in its basement, according to the State Emergency Service.
The destruction extended across residential, educational and medical facilities in the two districts.
Zelensky urges allies to accelerate air defense deliveries
Zelensky renewed his call for faster deliveries of Western air defense systems and ammunition, warning that delays were leaving Ukrainian cities vulnerable to further Russian missile strikes.
He said Ukraine continued to face a constant threat from ballistic missiles that could strike populated areas with little warning.
Under such circumstances, he argued, “artificial delays in providing air defense to Ukraine help terror.”
The president called for political agreements on defense assistance to be implemented promptly, stressing that Ukraine needed sufficient weapons not only to intercept incoming missiles but also to destroy Russian launchers.
The latest attack came amid an intensified Russian missile and drone campaign against Ukraine, with Kyiv’s residential neighborhoods, transport facilities, and civilian infrastructure repeatedly affected.

Captured Russian soldiers have a rule for one stretch of the Kupiansk front: go anywhere, but not there.
That stretch is the “safety corridor” the “Orion” unit of Ukraine’s Offensive Guard brigade “Pomsta” says it has built for its ground robots. The zone is so lethal that, by the unit’s count, 88% of attacking Russians are killed before they reach their positions, and Russian armor cannot get within 25 kilometers, the military outlet ArmyInform reports.
Behind that shield, the unit says its ground robots have run dozens of fully autonomous missions through the most dangerous ground on the axis, with a success rate of 99.57%. The results made Orion the top-ranked unit for effectiveness on the South-Kupiansk axis in September within Ukraine’s battlefield management system, DELTA.
“You can go anywhere, just not into the Orion zone”
The claim that the Russians now avoid the sector, the unit says, comes from them themselves.
“Prisoners admit in interviews: 'You can go anywhere, just not into the Orion zone.' Eighty-eight percent of the enemy is destroyed before reaching their positions, and Russian equipment cannot approach closer than 25 kilometers,” the unit says.
That is what opens the corridor. Where a human supply run would be a death sentence, a robot can cross, and cross again.
The quiet blood of the front
The point, the unit says, is to take the soldier out of the deadliest job on the front: carrying ammunition and the wounded across open fire.
“We broke the stereotype that supplying the army takes truck convoys and hundreds of soldiers under targeted fire. Our robotic systems are the ‘quiet blood’ of the front,” Vladyslav Zolotarov, an officer in the unit’s staff control group, says.
When Russia thinks our positions are depleted, a tracked platform quietly comes in at night and brings in a ton of ammunition.
In September alone, the unit says, its wheeled and tracked robots ran 85 of the hardest combat missions and hauled more than 30,000 kilograms of cargo. Its evacuation record is the line it is proudest of: four missions pulling wounded soldiers out by robot, all four successful, not one man lost.
Ukraine has bet heavily on this kind of machine, aiming to field 50,000 ground robots to keep its troops out of the drone-ruled kill zone.

articles.title: France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom (E5) agree to strengthen Europe’s role in NATO and maintain military support for Ukraine - Ejércitos
articles.summary: France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom (E5) agree to strengthen Europe’s role in NATO and maintain military support for Ukraine  Ejércitos
articles.full_text:
The defence ministers of France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom (E5) have reaffirmed in Paris their commitment to assuming greater responsibility for European security, strengthening military-industrial cooperation and maintaining support for Ukraine. The meeting, held in the format known as the E5, concluded with the adoption of a joint statement in which the participants identify Russia as the principal long-term threat to Euro-Atlantic stability and call for a greater European contribution to NATO's military capabilities. The document nevertheless stresses that this approach must be pursued in coordination with the United States, whose participation is regarded as indispensable to the Alliance's security.
The meeting was chaired by French Minister for the Armed Forces Catherine Vautrin and was also attended by the European Union's High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, Kaja Kallas, European Commissioner for Defence and Space Andrius Kubilius, and NATO Deputy Secretary General Radmila Shekerinska. The presence of representatives from both organisations made it possible to address the relationship between their respective initiatives, particularly with regard to capability requirements, industrial development and financing. According to the agenda published by NATO, the discussions were organised around two main issues: support for Ukraine and the security situation in the Middle East.
The E5 statement reflects a shared concern about the ability of European countries to respond to conventional, hybrid and multidomain threats. The ministers expressly mention violations of Allied airspace, acts of sabotage and other activities they consider part of a broader campaign of pressure against European states. The proposed response is to strengthen military readiness, modernise the armed forces and increase their ability to operate jointly. In addition, the published document links these priorities to the spending and capability-development commitments previously adopted by NATO in The Hague and reaffirmed in Ankara, although it establishes no new national budget targets and announces no additional funding allocations.
